l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Diodorus Siculus begins Book XI with Xerxes's expedition into Greece, which was planned with Mardonius's encouragement and coordinated with a Carthaginian invasion of Greece. Xerxes assembled a vast army and navy, crossed the Hellespont, and advanced through Thrace while the Grecian confederacy prepared defenses at Tempe, Thermopylae, and Artemisium. Leonidas commanded the Greek forces at Thermopylae, where they repeatedly defeated Persian attacks until a Trachinian revealed a mountain route that allowed the Persians to threaten their rear. The unit ends with the Greeks holding a midnight council to decide whether to abandon the pass.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Diodorus Siculus presents Book XI as a continuation of his history, beginning with Xerxes's expedition into Greece and ending the year before the Athenians under Cymon invaded Cyprus.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Greece was threatened by Xerxes's invasion and by a simultaneous Carthaginian attack on the Greeks in Italy and Sicily. Its cities were urged to unite in defense of their common liberty.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Persia prepared a massive land and naval expedition against Greece. The Persian king demanded earth and water from the Greek cities and accepted support from several Greek communities.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes resolved to invade Greece after Mardonius encouraged him and after learning of Carthaginian preparations. He built and gathered a huge fleet and army, crossed the Hellespont, marched through Thrace, and directed repeated attacks against Thermopylae.

l: Mardonius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Mardonius, a relative of Xerxes and a highly esteemed Persian commander, urged Xerxes to undertake the conquest and destruction of the Greeks. He desired command of the expedition.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Carthage agreed with Xerxes to attack the Greeks in Italy and Sicily while Xerxes invaded Greece. It spent three years raising troops and ships, assembling an army of three hundred thousand men and two hundred ships.

l: Carthaginian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The planned Carthaginian invasion was to occur at the same time as Xerxes's expedition. The Carthaginians intended to invade the Greeks in Italy and Sicily.

l: Xerxes's expedition into Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes's expedition was organized after the Persian defeat at Marathon and Darius's death prevented Darius from invading Greece. Xerxes marched from Susa to Sardis, crossed into Europe, and advanced toward the Greek defenses.

l: Battle of Marathon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Datis, Darius's general, had previously been defeated by the Athenians at Marathon. Darius thereafter bore an implacable hatred against Athens, but died before carrying out his planned invasion.

l: Sardis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes marched from Susa to Sardis and sent heralds from there into Greece to demand earth and water. He later marched from Sardis toward the Hellespont.

l: Hellespont, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes directed part of his forces to construct a bridge over the Hellespont. He later crossed with his army at Abydos and entered Europe.

l: Mount Athos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes sent another body of men to cut a passage through Mount Athos. The work was completed quickly and was intended to shorten and secure the army's route.

l: Thessaly, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Greeks sent ten thousand armed men into Thessaly to occupy the passages at Tempe. Much of Thessaly later submitted to the Persian commissioners, causing the Greek forces to withdraw.

l: Tempe, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Tempe was selected as a passage to be defended against the Persians. The Greek forces abandoned it after learning that most Thessalians and the inhabitants of the nearby straits had submitted to the king.

l: Themistocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Themistocles commanded the Athenian contingent sent toward Tempe. He and Synetus sent messengers to the Greek cities to raise soldiers at the common expense.

l: Doriscus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Xerxes brought his fleet to Doriscus so that his naval and land forces could join. There he numbered his forces, which included more than eight hundred thousand foot soldiers and more than twelve hundred galleys according to the account.

l: Artemisium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Grecian fleet was ordered to sail to Artemisium in Euboea. The Greeks judged it a convenient position from which to oppose the Persian navy.

l: Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Euboea contained Artemisium, where the Grecian fleet was ordered to assemble and oppose the enemy.

l: Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Thermopylae was occupied by Leonidas and a Greek force intended to secure its straits and passages. The defenders repelled successive Persian attacks until a local guide revealed a route around their position.

l: Battle of Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: At the Battle of Thermopylae, the Greek defenders used their close formation, large shields, and the narrow ground to defeat the Medes, Cissians, Sacians, and Persian troops called immortal. The battle turned when a Trachinian led twenty thousand Persians through a mountain pass to threaten Leonidas's rear.

l: Leonidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Leonidas, general of Sparta, commanded the Greek force at Thermopylae. He led a small but determined army that repeatedly defeated Persian assaults and then held a council after learning that the Persians were approaching from the rear.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Sparta sent Leonidas to command the defense of Thermopylae. Leonidas explained that the expedition was intended in truth to die for the common liberty and to advance the fame of Sparta.

l: Medes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Medes were placed at the front of the Persian attack at Thermopylae. They were defeated by the Greek formation, suffering heavy losses before the Cissians and Sacians continued the assault.

l: Hellespont bridge, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Hellespont bridge was constructed for Xerxes's army to pass from Asia into Europe. Xerxes crossed it at Abydos after the work had been completed.

l: Athos canal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Athos canal was cut through the isthmus by a large labor force. It enabled Xerxes's fleet to pass into the other sea by a shorter and safer route.

l: Grecian cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Grecian confederacy organized common resistance to Xerxes and ordered forces toward Tempe, Thermopylae, and Artemisium. It threatened that Greek communities supporting Persia would be punished if Greece prevailed.

l: Greek fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Grecian fleet was ordered to sail to Artemisium in Euboea to oppose the Persian fleet. Eurybiades, a Lacedaemonian, served as its admiral.

l: Persian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Persian army crossed the Hellespont, marched through Thrace, and was reinforced by Thracians and other borderers. At Thermopylae it suffered repeated defeats despite its overwhelming numbers.

l: Persian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: The Persian navy included more than twelve hundred galleys, along with ships for transporting horses and thousands of cargo vessels. It sailed alongside the army and passed through the Athos canal.

l: Greek liberty, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, LAST TEN BOOKS / BOOK XI.
s: Greek liberty was presented as the common cause for which the Greek cities were urged to unite. Leonidas's soldiers declared that they preferred to fight armed for their liberty rather than accept Persian promises of land and safety.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, ordered most of the Greek forces to depart while the Lacedaemonians and Thespians remained to defend the straits. After eating, the remaining Greeks attacked the Persian camp at night, causing confusion and heavy losses among the Persians. Xerxes escaped from his pavilion, which the Greeks entered while searching for him. At daybreak, the Persians surrounded and killed Leonidas’s men with darts and arrows, but they died defending Greece’s liberty and honour.

l: Leonidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, ordered the other forces to depart and kept the Lacedaemonians and Thespians with him. He led his remaining men in a night attack on the Persian camp and was among those destroyed after the Persians surrounded them at daybreak.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Lacedaemonians were ordered by Leonidas to remain and not desert the defence of the straits. Together with the Thespians, they numbered fewer than five hundred and died fighting for the liberty and glory of Greece.

l: Thespians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Thespians were kept with Leonidas after the other forces departed. They joined the Lacedaemonians in the night attack and were destroyed with them by the Persians.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Greeks who remained at the pass chose honour before life and asked Leonidas to lead them against the Persians. They attacked the Persian camp at night, killed many enemies, searched for Xerxes, and were ultimately destroyed.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Persians were thrown into fear and confusion by the unexpected Greek attack, and many were killed by the Greeks and by one another. At daybreak, they surrounded the few remaining Greeks and destroyed them with darts and arrows.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Xerxes escaped from his pavilion at the beginning of the tumult and got out of harm’s way. The Greeks entered his pavilion, killed almost everyone they found there, and searched for him throughout the Persian camp.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Greeks sacrificed their lives for the common safety of Greece. They preferred to die valiantly and honourably rather than live as slaves and in disgrace.

l: Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Lacedaemonians and Thespians guarded the passes in Thermopylae. They refused to desert their assigned post and were destroyed while defending it.

l: the straits, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Leonidas ordered the Lacedaemonians not to desert the defence of the straits. The remaining Greeks fought there rather than withdraw.

l: Persian camp, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The remaining Greeks rushed into the Persian camp at night and advanced toward the king’s pavilion. The attack caused widespread confusion and slaughter before the Persians surrounded the Greeks at daybreak.

l: defence of the straits, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Leonidas directed the Lacedaemonians to remain for the defence of the straits. The defenders chose to die at their post rather than abandon it.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: The Greek attack might have ended the war if Xerxes had been killed in his pavilion. Xerxes escaped, and the fighting ended with the destruction of Leonidas’s remaining forces.

l: Greek liberty and honour, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, But Leonidas, the Lacedaemonian general, anxious to obtajii
s: Leonidas and his men chose honour before life and prepared to die for the liberty and glory of Greece. Their final stand was presented as a sacrifice for the common safety of Greece.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The unit concerns the five hundred defenders at Thermopylae, who faced an enormously larger Persian force without hope of victory but with determination to defend Greece's laws and liberty. Their defeat and death are presented as a greater source of fame than many victories because their courage rested on firm resolutions rather than fortune. Their stand astonished and discouraged the Persians while inspiring the Greeks, and poets including Simonides celebrated their sacrifice. Leonidas, identified as the Spartan king, is singled out as proof that true valour cannot die.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The Persians were terrified and amazed by the incredible attempt of five hundred defenders to attack a vastly larger force. Their astonishment discouraged them in later fighting, leaving them with little heart to fight.

l: five hundred defenders (at Thermopylae), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The five hundred defenders attacked an immense multitude despite having no hope of overcoming it, choosing to defend their country's laws rather than preserve their lives. Although surrounded by dangers and exhausted in body, they remained unconquerable in mind and became a lasting example of valour.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The Greeks were inspired by the defenders and became eager to gain similar honour with their countrymen. Their spirits were inflamed by the example of the five hundred.

l: common liberty of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The common liberty of Greece is said to owe more to the defenders' stand than to those who later overcame Xerxes in battle, because their extraordinary attempt discouraged the Persians and encouraged the Greeks.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: Xerxes is mentioned as the ruler whom the Greeks later overcame in following battles. The unit maintains that the defenders' earlier stand contributed more to the common liberty of Greece than those later victories.

l: Leonidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: Leonidas is identified as the Spartan king and is singled out in Simonides' poem. He is presented as having shown posterity that real valour cannot die.

l: Battle of Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The battle of Thermopylae is represented through the defenders' unequal stand against the Persians and their honourable death. Its memory was preserved by historians and poets, including Simonides.

l: the defenders' death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The defenders' death brought them greater fame than others gained through glorious victories. Their tomb is described in Simonides' poem as an altar and memorial whose honour would survive time.

l: valour, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: Valour is judged by solid and well-grounded resolutions rather than by the event, since fortune controls outcomes while reason supports deliberate courage. The defenders' valour is presented as unparalleled and enduring.

l: fame and glory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, On the other hand, this terror and amazement of the Persians
s: The defenders sought fame and glory by attempting what had never been done before, even though they expected no victory. Their memory and praise were preserved by historians and poets, and their defeat made them more famous than others' victories.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Xerxes captured the passes after Thermopylae and sent the Persian fleet against the Grecians, but storms and fighting at Artemisium reduced Persian strength. Themistocles advised the Grecians to fight in confined waters, first at Artemisium and later at Salamis, where the Greek fleet defeated the Persian fleet. After Athens was burned and the Persian army devastated parts of Greece, Themistocles used false reports about the bridge to persuade Xerxes to withdraw to Asia, leaving Mardonius with a large army.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Xerxes gained the passes after Thermopylae and ordered Megabates to attack the Grecian fleet. He led his army through Phocia, Boeotia, and Attica, where towns and temples were destroyed, including Athens. After the defeat at Salamis, he believed Themistocles' report that the Grecians intended to destroy the bridge and withdrew to Asia, leaving Mardonius with an army of four hundred thousand men.

l: Themistocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Themistocles directed matters concerning the Greek fleet and advised attacking the Persians before they could assemble. He argued for fighting at Salamis because the narrow straits favored the Grecians, and he helped arrange the fleet for battle. He later sent a false message to Xerxes claiming that the Grecians intended to destroy the bridge, causing Xerxes to withdraw.

l: Eurybiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Eurybiades, a Spartan, served as admiral of the Greek fleet. He and Themistocles encouraged the Grecians and arranged the fleet for the battle at Salamis.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Grecians fought the Persians at sea near Artemisium and later at Salamis. After Athens was destroyed, they gathered at Salamis and debated where to fight, eventually defeating the Persian fleet in the narrow straits. They lost forty ships at Salamis while sinking about two hundred Persian galleys.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Persians lost many soldiers at Thermopylae and many ships to storms and battles. Their fleet was defeated at Salamis after confusion developed in the narrow straits, and many Persian ships were sunk or captured.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Athenians supplied one hundred and forty ships for the Greek fleet and fought bravely at Artemisium and Salamis. They evacuated their wives, children, and possessions to Salamis before Athens was destroyed. At Salamis, they attacked the Phoenician and Cyprian ships and pursued the fleeing Persians.

l: Peloponnesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Peloponnesians favored fighting near the isthmus so that they could withdraw into Peloponnesus if necessary. They helped enclose the isthmus with a wall extending from Lechaeum to Cenchreae.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Athens was abandoned by its inhabitants as the Persians advanced. Xerxes razed the city and burned its temples, including the temple of Pallas.

l: Salamis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Salamis became the refuge of the Athenians and the station of the Grecian fleet after the fleet withdrew from Artemisium. The Grecians fought the Persians in its straits and won a major naval victory there.

l: Euboea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Grecian fleet was stationed at Artemisium in Euboea. The Persian fleet later took Istiaea in Euboea by storm, razed it, and devastated the island and its surrounding country.

l: Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Thermopylae was the site where the Persians gained the passes at great cost. News of the defeat and slaughter there discouraged the Grecians and influenced their later decisions.

l: Peloponnesus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Peloponnesus received the inhabitants who withdrew from Athens, Boeotia, and other threatened regions. The Peloponnesians regarded it as a place of safety and defense and fortified its isthmus.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The unit describes the Persian invasion of Greece, including the destruction of Greek towns and temples and the naval fighting at Artemisium and Salamis. After the victory at Salamis, the affairs of Greece are presented as having turned in favor of the Grecians.

l: Greek naval victory at Salamis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Grecians won a decisive naval victory at Salamis after the Persian fleet lost order in the narrow straits. The Grecians lost forty ships, while about two hundred Persian galleys were sunk, with others captured.

l: Battle of Thermopylae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Battle of Thermopylae ended with Xerxes gaining the passes and the slaughter of the defending valiant men. The Grecians later remembered the defeat and were discouraged by it.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: During the invasion, Xerxes' forces devastated Phocia, Boeotia, and Attica, destroyed Platea, and burned Athens and its temples. Persian forces also attacked the Grecian fleet, but storms and the defeat at Salamis weakened their campaign.

l: Greek fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Greek fleet fought the Persian fleet near Artemisium and later withdrew to Salamis. Under Eurybiades and Themistocles, it was arranged to exploit the narrow straits and defeated the Persians there.

l: Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: The Persian fleet suffered heavy losses in a storm near Sepias and later in battles near Artemisium. At Salamis, it entered the straits in disorder, lost its leading admiral, and was driven into flight after many ships were sunk or captured.

l: Greek defensive strategy at Salamis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Themistocles argued that the Grecians should fight inside the straits of Salamis, where a smaller fleet could oppose the larger Persian force. The Grecian commanders arranged their ships in the straits and used the confined waters to disrupt the Persian fleet.

l: Themistocles' deception of Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now said enough of these gallant men, we shall return
s: Themistocles sent his children's schoolmaster to tell Xerxes that the Grecians were sailing toward the bridge to destroy it. Xerxes believed the report, feared that his return to Asia would be blocked, and withdrew with his forces, leaving Mardonius behind.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Carthaginians invaded Sicily under Amilcar and besieged Himera, but Gelon of Syracuse defeated them through a stratagem that killed Amilcar and burned their fleet. The Carthaginian army suffered massive losses, while many survivors surrendered after being deprived of water. Gelon received widespread praise, treated the defeated Sicilians and Carthaginians generously, and made peace with Carthage in exchange for tribute and the construction of two temples. The victory at Himera was said to have occurred on the same day that Leonidas and the Greeks fought at Thermopylae during the Persian invasion of Greece.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Carthaginians invaded Sicily with a large army and fleet under Amilcar, but Gelon defeated them at Himera. They lost vast numbers of men, and their surviving leaders sent ambassadors to Gelon to seek peace. They agreed to pay two thousand talents of silver and build two temples, and promised a gold crown to Demareta.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Persians had agreed with the Carthaginians to attack the Greeks in Sicily at the same time that the Carthaginians invaded. The Persian king and many more troops escaped, unlike the Carthaginian army.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Greeks were to be attacked simultaneously by the Persians and the Carthaginians according to their agreement. News of Gelon's victory encouraged the Greeks, who were fighting at Thermopylae.

l: Sicilians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Sicilians were initially terrified by the size of the barbarian forces, but Gelon's victory restored their courage. They honored Gelon, who later behaved with modesty and humanity toward them.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Amilcar was chosen as general of the Carthaginian forces and led the invasion of Sicily. Gelon sent horsemen disguised as Selinuntian allies into the Carthaginian naval camp, where they killed Amilcar during a sacrifice and set fire to the ships.

l: Gelon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Gelon marched from Syracuse to relieve Himera with fifty thousand foot soldiers and five thousand horse. He used cavalry raids and a stratagem involving disguised horsemen to kill Amilcar and burn the Carthaginian fleet, then defeated the Carthaginian army. He was praised throughout Sicily, made peace with Carthage, built temples from the spoils, and was proclaimed benefactor, king, and deliverer of his country by the Syracusans.

l: Theron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Theron, prince of the Agrigentines, was responsible for the defense of Himera but became frightened by the Carthaginian advance. He sent urgently to Gelon at Syracuse for reinforcements and had previously built gates because of fear of the enemy.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Carthage sent a large expedition to Sicily, but the defeat at Himera caused widespread fear, mourning, and lamentation in the city. Its ambassadors later secured peace with Gelon by accepting his financial and religious conditions.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Sicily was invaded by the Carthaginians, who attempted to conquer Himera. After Gelon's victory, the island was described as appearing to have all Africa under its dominion because of the many prisoners and slaves.

l: Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Himera was besieged by the Carthaginian army after Amilcar landed at Panormus and marched against it. Gelon's arrival revived the city's defenders, and the Carthaginians were ultimately defeated and driven from the area.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Syracuse sent Gelon and a large force to relieve Himera. After the victory, Gelon returned there and was accepted by the armed citizens as their benefactor, king, and deliverer.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Greece was the intended target of the Persian attack that was coordinated with the Carthaginian invasion of Sicily. Gelon planned to cross into Greece and join the Greeks against the Persians, but he abandoned the plan after hearing of the Greek victory at Salamis.

l: Battle of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Battle of Himera ended in a decisive Sicilian victory achieved through Gelon's plan to kill Amilcar and burn the Carthaginian ships. About one hundred and fifty thousand Carthaginians were said to have been slain, while others surrendered because they lacked water.

l: Carthaginian invasion of Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The invasion was prepared in coordination with the Persian attack on the Greeks and involved at least three hundred thousand land troops, more than two thousand warships, and over three thousand transports. It ended with the destruction or capture of the invading army and the subsequent peace between Carthage and Gelon.

l: siege of Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: During the siege, Amilcar established separate land and naval camps, fortified the area, and blocked Himera from the west. Gelon's arrival enabled the defenders to attack the dispersed Carthaginian forces and eventually destroy the siege.

l: Carthaginian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Carthaginian army numbered no less than three hundred thousand and was divided between camps near Himera. It was routed after Amilcar was killed and the fleet was burned; roughly one hundred and fifty thousand were slain, and the remainder either reached a naturally fortified place or surrendered.

l: Carthaginian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Carthaginian fleet contained more than two thousand warships and over three thousand transport ships, although a storm destroyed the vessels carrying the horses and chariots. Gelon's disguised horsemen later burned the ships in the naval camp, and the twenty ships that escaped were eventually wrecked except for a few men who reached Carthage in a small boat.

l: peace treaty between Gelon and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: Gelon made peace with Carthage after receiving its tearful ambassadors. The agreement required Carthage to pay two thousand talents of silver and build two temples where the terms of the league could be preserved as sacred.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. U.
s: The Persian invasion of Greece was coordinated with the Carthaginian attack on Sicily. The same day as Gelon's victory at Himera, Leonidas and the Greeks fought at Thermopylae; later, news of the Greek victory at Salamis caused Gelon to abandon his plan to send forces to Greece.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: After the Persian fleet withdrew from Salamis to Samos, the Athenians rejected Persian offers and reaffirmed their alliance with the Greeks. Mardonius invaded Attica, forcing the Athenians to evacuate to Salamis, and destroyed Athens and its remaining temples. The Greek confederacy assembled at Plataea under Pausanias and Aristides, defeated the larger Persian army, killed Mardonius, and drove the Persians from Greece. The Greeks buried their dead, distributed the spoils, honored Pausanias, and later punished the Theban leaders who had supported the Persians.

l: victory of the Greeks over Mardonius at Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Greeks defeated Mardonius and the Persian army at Plataea after a battle in which Mardonius was killed and the Persians were routed. More than one hundred thousand barbarians were reportedly put to the sword, while the Greeks lost more than ten thousand men.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Greeks formed a confederate army, swore to prosecute the war and defend their liberty, and marched into Boeotia. They defeated the Persians at Plataea, buried their dead, divided the spoils, and dedicated a tenth of the spoils at Delphi.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Persians offered the Athenians territory, restored walls and temples, and the enjoyment of their former laws and liberties if they would ally with Persia. Their army was defeated at Plataea, although Artabazus led about forty thousand men safely back into Asia.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Athenians were credited with much of the success at Salamis but resented being denied the chief honor. They rejected Persian proposals, evacuated Attica twice, fought at Plataea, helped defeat the Persians, and later established funeral games for those who died in the war.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Lacedaemonians sought to restrain Athens and secured honors for the men of Aegina and for Amynias at Salamis. They eventually joined the defense of Attica, fought the Persian forces at Plataea, and under Pausanias besieged the Persian camp and later marched against Thebes.

l: Mardonius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Mardonius attempted to win over the cities of the Peloponnesus and then invaded Attica with a large army after the Athenians rejected Persian terms. He destroyed Athens and its remaining temples, fought at Plataea, and was killed while leading the Persian forces.

l: Aristides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Aristides commanded the Athenians at Plataea. He sent Athenian troops to aid the Megareans against the Persian cavalry, and the relief force killed the Persian cavalry commander and routed his men.

l: Pausanias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Pausanias, described as the tutor of Leonidas, commanded the Greek army because Leonidas was under age. He helped lead the victory at Plataea, ordered that no Persian prisoners be taken, received the greatest honor among the Greek commanders, and later ordered the execution of the leading Theban supporters of Persia.

l: Artabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Artabazus commanded the Persian survivors who fled from Plataea by a shorter route through Phocis. He led more than forty thousand men through Macedonia and brought them safely into Asia.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Athens received Persian and Lacedaemonian ambassadors after the Athenians had been slighted by the other Greeks. Mardonius later destroyed the city and its temples, and the Athenians subsequently commemorated their war dead with public burials and funeral games.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Attica was invaded by Mardonius with a large Persian force. Its inhabitants abandoned the country with their families and possessions, fleeing to Salamis, after which Mardonius devastated the region.

l: Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Plataea was chosen as the place where the Greek confederacy would confront the Persians for the liberty of Greece. The Greeks vowed to establish a festival and athletic contests there if they were victorious.

l: Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: After the battle at Salamis, the Persian fleet, except for the Phoenicians, wintered near Cuma and then sailed to Samos to guard the Ionian coasts. It consisted of four hundred ships and closely watched the Ionian cities because the Persians distrusted the Ionians.

l: Greek army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Greek army numbered about one hundred thousand men and was commanded at Plataea by Pausanias and Aristides. It used a defensible position between a hill and the Asopus River, defeated the Persian army, and then divided into groups to pursue the fleeing enemy.

l: Persian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Persian army was described as numbering five hundred thousand men and was supported by cavalry and a fortified timber camp. It initially fought with courage, but after Mardonius was killed it lost heart, fled, and suffered immense losses.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Thebans had supported Mardonius and sheltered Persian forces that fled from Plataea. They defended Thebes against the Greek assault, but their city was eventually entered, and the principal authors of their alliance with Persia were surrendered and executed.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: Thebes sheltered the Greek allies of Mardonius and Persian fugitives after the battle. The Greek army later marched against the city, entered it after fighting, and compelled the leading supporters of Persia to surrender.

l: Salamis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: After the battle at Salamis, the Persian fleet withdrew to Cuma and later Samos. The Athenians also fled to Salamis when Mardonius invaded Attica.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Persian invasion led to the destruction of Athens and its temples and forced the Athenians to abandon Attica. The invasion was resisted by the Greek confederacy, which defeated Mardonius at Plataea.

l: Grecian cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. HI.
s: The Greek confederacy resolved to join the Athenians and march to Plataea against the Persians. Its members swore not to prefer life to liberty, not to abandon their officers or fallen soldiers, and not to rebuild temples destroyed by the barbarians.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Leotychides the Lacedaemonian and Xantippus the Athenian led the Greek fleet from Samos toward Mycale to help the Asian Greeks regain their liberty. The Persian fleet withdrew to shore, fortified its camp, and summoned a large land force, but the Persians were defeated after the Samians, Milesians, and other Asian peoples joined the battle. The victory at Mycale, occurring on the same day as the Greek victory at Plataea, resulted in the slaughter or dispersal of the Persian army. Afterward, the Ionians and Eolians were received as Greek confederates, but they ultimately remained in Asia, while the Athenians captured Sestos before returning to Athens.

l: Leotychides the Lacedaemonian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Leotychides the Lacedaemonian commanded the Greek fleet with Xantippus the Athenian. He led the fleet to Mycale, used a herald to encourage revolt among the Greeks serving the Persians, directed the Greek army in battle, pursued the defeated Persians, and later received the Ionians and Eolians as confederates.

l: Xantippus the Athenian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Xantippus the Athenian commanded the Greek fleet with Leotychides the Lacedaemonian. He took part in the battle at Mycale, pursued the defeated Persians, and later helped receive the Ionians and Eolians as confederates.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Xerxes was said by the Persians to be approaching with a great army, which they used to encourage their soldiers. After learning of the Persian defeats at Plataea and Mycale, he fled with part of his forces to Ecbatana, leaving other forces to continue the war.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Greeks sent a fleet to assist the inhabitants of Asia in regaining their liberty. They fought the Persians at Mycale, defeated and pursued them, and later accepted the Ionians and Eolians as confederates.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Persians withdrew their fleet to shore, fortified it with a wall and trench, and summoned a large land force. They fought the Greeks at Mycale but were defeated and dispersed, suffering the slaughter of forty thousand men.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Athenians later persuaded the Ionians and Eolians to remain in Asia, promising to send them aid because of their kinship and connection with Athens. They feared that if the Ionians moved elsewhere, the Ionians would no longer regard Athens as their metropolitan city, and they later captured Sestos and returned to Athens.

l: Ionians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Ionians sought assistance from the Greek commanders so that the Asian cities could regain their liberty. They served with the Persians but considered revolt, and after the battle they were received as Greek confederates; although initially persuaded to move to Europe, they ultimately decided to remain in Asia.

l: Eolians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Eolians joined the Greeks during the defeat of the Persians at Mycale and helped slaughter the fleeing Persians. They were afterward received as confederates and were initially persuaded to prepare to move to Europe, but they remained in Asia after the Athenians changed their advice.

l: Samians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Samians joined the Greek forces at Mycale and marched swiftly toward the enemy. Their arrival revived the courage of the Greeks and contributed to the Persian defeat.

l: Milesians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Milesians joined the Samians in advancing against the Persians at Mycale. Their appearance helped revive the courage of the Greeks and contributed to the Persian rout.

l: battle of Mycale, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The battle of Mycale was fought between the Greeks and Persians on the same day as the battle at Plataea. The Greeks defeated the Persians, who suffered the slaughter of forty thousand men, while many others fled to their camp or to Sardis.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Medean war ended after two years with the battle of Mycale, the taking of Sestos, and the return of the Lacedaemonians and Athenians to their homes.

l: Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Persian fleet departed from Samos after hearing of the Greek expedition and withdrew to Mycale because it was considered too weak to face the Greeks. Its ships were hauled ashore and protected by a wall and a deep trench.

l: Greek fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Greek fleet, commanded by Leotychides the Lacedaemonian and Xantippus the Athenian, sailed from Delos toward Mycale with 250 galleys. It supported the battle against the Persians and afterward sailed back to Samos.

l: Samos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Samos sent ambassadors to the Greek commanders asking them to assist the inhabitants of Asia. The Persian fleet withdrew from Samos to Mycale, and after the battle the Greek commanders returned to Samos, where they received the Ionians and Eolians as confederates.

l: Mycale, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Mycale was the place where the Persian fleet was drawn ashore and fortified before the battle. The Greeks defeated the Persian army there, and the victory helped bring the Asian cities toward revolt and liberty.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Athens was regarded by the Ionians as their metropolitan city and place of origin. The Athenians persuaded the Ionians and Eolians to remain in Asia and later returned to Athens after capturing Sestos.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Asia contained the Greek cities whose inhabitants sought to regain their liberty from Persian control. The Ionians and Eolians considered moving to Europe but ultimately remained in Asia after receiving assurances of assistance from the Athenians.

l: liberty of the Asian cities, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The liberty of the Asian cities was the stated purpose of the Greek expedition from Delos. The victory at Mycale encouraged the Asian cities to revolt, and many inhabitants joined the Greeks against the Persians.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: After the victory at Plataea, the Athenians rebuilt the walls of Athens, despite opposition from the Lacedaemonians, and Themistocles secured their completion through diplomacy and deception. Themistocles later promoted the enlargement of the harbor at Piraeus, the expansion of the Athenian fleet, and policies to attract foreign residents and artisans. Pausanias, the Spartan commander, was exposed for conspiring with the Persians, while Aristides gained the allegiance of the Greek cities through his justice and moderation. Aristides also established a common war fund at Delos and administered contributions totaling 560 talents.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: After the victory at Plataea, Athens received its returning women and children and began repairing its walls. The city later enlarged its harbor, expanded its fleet, and gained leadership over the Greek cities through Aristides's conduct.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The Athenians rebuilt their walls with the help of women, children, strangers, and servants, using materials taken from houses and sepulchres. They later completed the harbor works, planned to add twenty galleys each year, and gained the submission of the Greek cities.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The Lacedaemonians opposed the fortification of Athens and attempted to stop the work through ambassadors and threats. They later lost command at sea after Pausanias's misconduct, while Aristides won the allegiance of the allied cities for the Athenians.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Sparta detained Themistocles and his fellow ambassadors while sending officials to inspect the walls of Athens, but was compelled to release them after the Athenian ambassadors detained Spartan representatives. Sparta later ordered Pausanias to free Greek cities from Persian garrisons and eventually punished him for treason.

l: Themistocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Themistocles advised the Athenians to continue fortifying Athens while he delayed and deceived the Lacedaemonians. He later planned the enlargement of the harbor at Piraeus, persuaded the people to expand the fleet, and promoted the admission of foreign residents and artisans.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The Greeks were presented as threatened by possible further Persian invasions. Greek cities formerly under Persian control were freed, and many later placed themselves under Athenian protection because of Aristides's conduct.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The Persians maintained garrisons in some Greek cities until Pausanias removed them. Persian officials, including Artabazus, secretly supplied Pausanias with money, and Pausanias conspired to betray Greece and marry the king's daughter.

l: Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Plataea is identified as the place of a Greek victory after which the Athenians returned their families to Athens and rebuilt the city's walls. Pausanias had also commanded at Plataea before undertaking later operations against Persian garrisons.

l: victory at Plataea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The victory at Plataea preceded the Athenians' return to Athens and their rapid effort to repair and strengthen the city's defenses. Pausanias's reputation and authority had also grown because of this victory and his other actions.

l: walls of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The walls of Athens were rebuilt after the victory at Plataea despite Lacedaemonian opposition. The Athenians completed them quickly through the labor of the whole population, and the work increased Themistocles's honor among the citizens.

l: fortification of Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The fortification of Athens was opposed by the Lacedaemonians, who claimed that walled cities could serve as Persian strongholds in a future invasion. Themistocles delayed their intervention while the Athenians completed the work.

l: Phaleron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Phaleron served as the Athenians' port because the Piraeus was said to lack a suitable harbor. Themistocles sought to replace its use by developing a larger and more convenient harbor at Piraeus.

l: Piraeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Piraeus was described as lacking a harbor suitable for the Athenians' needs. Themistocles planned to turn it into a spacious and beautiful harbor that would strengthen Athenian power at sea.

l: harbor at Piraeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The harbor at Piraeus was planned by Themistocles as a spacious, beautiful, and economical harbor. It was completed in a short time and was intended to help make the Athenians masters of the seas.

l: Athenian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: The Athenian fleet had already won many victories at sea and was regarded by Themistocles as the foundation of greater Athenian power. He advised the Athenians to add twenty galleys to it every year.

l: Aristides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Aristides joined Themistocles's plan as a trusted evaluator and judged it beneficial to the commonwealth. He later served as admiral, gained the confidence of the Greek cities through his justice and moderation, established the common fund at Delos, and administered its contributions fairly.

l: Delos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Delos was selected as the location of a common treasury where money collected for public service would be kept. Under Aristides's administration, the contributions reached 560 talents.

l: Pausanias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Pausanias, the Lacedaemonian commander at Plataea, freed cities from Persian garrisons and took Byzantium. He later accepted Persian luxury, acted tyrannically, conspired with Artabazus to betray Greece, was exposed, and died after being sealed inside the temple of Minerva Chalcidica.

l: Pausanias's treason, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Pausanias's treason consisted of a secret agreement with Artabazus and Xerxes to betray Greece in exchange for wealth and marriage to the king's daughter. The conspiracy was revealed through intercepted letters and a staged conversation, leading to Pausanias's death and Sparta's loss of command at sea.

l: Aristides's administration of the war fund, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, I.
s: Aristides's administration of the war fund was marked by justice and integrity. He organized contributions from the allied cities, totaling 560 talents, and distributed the money so fairly that all the cities approved his decisions.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hiero of Syracuse prepared to attack Theron and Polyzelus at Agrigentum, but exposed a Himeraean plot against Theron and reconciled with him. Hiero expelled the Cataneans and Naxians, founded Aetna, and later defeated the Etruscans at sea. The Tarentines were defeated by the Japyges, while Thrasideus lost a war against Hiero, abdicated, and killed himself; three hundred Fabii were also slain at Cremera. Themistocles was accused, ostracized, forced into exile, received by Xerxes in Persia, and died at Magnesia after a career praised for saving Greece from the Persian invasion.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Athens ostracized Themistocles after he became suspected and envied because of his popularity. The city had earlier benefited greatly from his counsels and services in the Persian invasion of Greece.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Sparta was said to have been contemned because of Pausanias's treachery, while Athens became famous for loyalty. A Spartan senator, Hetaemaridas, persuaded the city not to wage war against Athens for dominion of the sea.

l: Hiero, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hiero, king of Syracuse, feared the influence of his brother Polyzelus and sought to remove him by sending him to command an army. He later exposed the Himeraeans' plot against Theron, expelled the Cataneans and Naxians, defeated the Etruscans at sea, and defeated Thrasideus in war.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Syracuse was ruled by Hiero and supplied the force that defeated Thrasideus. Its army lost two thousand men in that battle, while the opposing side lost more than four thousand.

l: Polyzelus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Polyzelus suspected that Hiero had given him command of an army so that he would die in battle and therefore refused the command. He fled to Theron, and after the Himeraean plot was exposed Theron restored him to his brother's former love and favor.

l: Theron, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Theron, king of Agrigentum, received Polyzelus when he fled from Hiero and was later reconciled with Hiero after the Himeraean conspiracy was revealed. He governed with moderation and justice, died in the sixteenth year of his reign, and was revered as a divine hero.

l: Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Agrigentum was ruled by Theron and became involved in conflict with Syracuse under Thrasideus. After Thrasideus's defeat and death, its people restored their democratic government and sent ambassadors to Hiero to seek peace.

l: Thrasideus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Thrasideus, son of Theron, governed Himera harshly and later ruled Agrigentum tyrannically after succeeding his father. He led an army against the Syracusans, was defeated, abdicated, fled to the Megarensians, and killed himself after being condemned to die.

l: Himera, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The people of Himera, alienated by Thrasideus's harsh government, offered to surrender their city to Hiero and assist him against Theron. Hiero revealed their plot, and Theron put many of the traitors to death; he later settled Dorians in the largely depopulated city.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Lacedaemonians considered war against the Athenians to recover dominion of the sea, but Hetaemaridas persuaded them to desist. They later accused Themistocles of conspiring with Pausanias and sought to have him tried by a general Greek council.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Athenians feared war with the Spartans, built many galleys, gathered treasure, and sought allies, but abandoned these preparations when they learned that the Lacedaemonians would not fight. They later ostracized Themistocles despite his former services.

l: Tyrrhenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Etruscans of Tyrrhenia fought Hiero's fleet after the citizens of Cuma requested assistance. Several of their ships were sunk, and their sea power was broken.

l: Tarentines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Tarentines fought the Japyges over the boundaries of their lands. They were defeated, divided during the pursuit, and driven toward Tarentum and Rhegium.

l: Japyges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Japyges brought more than twenty thousand men into the field against the Tarentines and their allies. They won the battle, pursued the defeated forces, and captured Rhegium.

l: war between the Tarentines and Japyges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The war began over the limits of the Tarentines' and Japyges' lands. After initial skirmishes and mutual plundering, it escalated into open war, ending in a Japyge victory and the capture of Rhegium.

l: Syracusan-Agrigentine war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Hiero and Thrasideus fought after Thrasideus raised an army of more than twenty thousand horse and foot. Hiero wasted the borders of Agrigentum and defeated Thrasideus's forces, with two thousand Syracusans and more than four thousand of the opposing side killed.

l: three hundred Fabii massacre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: During Rome's war with the Veientes, the Romans were routed in a battle at Cremera. Three hundred Fabii, all members of one family, were among those killed.

l: Themistocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Themistocles was accused by the Lacedaemonians of conspiring with Pausanias, but was acquitted at Athens before later being ostracized. He fled through Admetus's territory to Asia, was received by Xerxes, acquired Magnesia, Myus, and Lampsacus, and died at Magnesia; the text praises him as the foremost of the Greeks for saving Greece and advancing Athens.

l: Pausanias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Pausanias was remembered for treachery and was used by the Lacedaemonians in their accusations against Themistocles. He had allegedly solicited Themistocles to join him in betraying Greece to Xerxes.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Xerxes received Themistocles after he arrived in Persia and, after hearing his defense, acquitted and honored him. One account says Xerxes later wanted to renew the war against Greece and asked Themistocles to command the army.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: The Persians were defeated by the Greeks in the sea fight in which Mandona lost her children. Themistocles later reached Persia, learned the Persian language, and was acquitted before the Persian senate.

l: ostracism, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Ostracism at Athens required citizens to write on shells the name of a person they feared might overturn the popular government. The person named most often was banished for five years, ostensibly to humble powerful and aspiring men.

l: Admetus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Admetus, king of the Molossians, initially received the fugitive Themistocles courteously and promised to protect him. Under pressure from the Lacedaemonians, he gave Themistocles money and advised him to leave secretly.

l: Magnesia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Magnesia, near the river Meander and rich in corn, was given to Themistocles by Xerxes for his support. Themistocles lived there and died there, and a sumptuous monument was erected over his burial place.

l: Themistocles's exile and death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Themistocles's exile began with his ostracism from Athens and continued through flight to Admetus and then to Persia. He was honored by Xerxes, lived in Magnesia with great abundance, and died there; another account says he drank bull's blood and immediately died after refusing to lead a renewed Persian war against Greece.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. VII.
s: Themistocles was praised for opposing the combined strength of Asia, defeating the Persians, preserving Greece during the war, and using a stratagem involving the destruction of a bridge to divide the enemy's land forces.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Cimon led the Athenians in campaigns against the Persians, capturing cities in Asia and winning victories at Cyprus and Eurymedon by sea and land. A devastating earthquake struck Sparta, after which the Helots and Messenians revolted and besieged Ithome, while the Argives destroyed Mycenae. In Sicily, Hiero died, Thrasybulus was overthrown by a Syracusan revolt, and democracy was restored in Syracuse. Artabanus arranged the murder of Xerxes, but Artaxerxes killed Artabanus and became king of Persia.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Athens chose Cimon, the son of Miltiades, as general and sent him with a large army to aid the confederate cities in Asia. The city gained wealth, power, and fame from the victories over the Persians.

l: Cimon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Cimon captured Eion and Scyros, conquered Persian-held cities in Caria and Lycia, and commanded victories at Cyprus and Eurymedon. He used captured Persian ships disguised with Persian ornaments to surprise the Persian land army.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Athenians sent Cimon to free the confederate cities in Asia and defeated the Persians at sea and on land. They dedicated a tenth of the spoils to their gods and became wealthier and more powerful.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Persians lost cities in Caria and Lycia, a naval battle at Cyprus, and a land battle at Eurymedon. They lost ships, soldiers, prisoners, and treasure, and afterward began building more ships because of their fear of the Athenians.

l: Caria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Grecian cities on the coast of Caria revolted from the Persians when Cimon arrived. Cimon stormed the cities that retained their native inhabitants and Persian garrisons, bringing Caria under his power.

l: Cyprus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Persian fleet was stationed at Cyprus when Cimon sailed there and joined battle. After the Athenian victory, the Persian soldiers fled ashore and the remaining ships came into the hands of the enemy.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Xerxes was king of Persia for twenty years. Artabanus and Mithridates arranged his murder, after which Artabanus falsely accused Darius of the killing.

l: Eurymedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Persian land army was encamped at Eurymedon. Cimon attacked it at night after disguising captured Persian ships and troops, routing the army and killing Pheredates.

l: battle at Cyprus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Cimon fought the Persian fleet with 250 ships against 340 Persian ships. The Athenians won, taking more than 100 ships and their crews while sinking or destroying many others.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Sparta suffered a devastating earthquake that overturned houses and killed more than twenty thousand people. Afterward, the Helots and Messenians made war against the weakened city.

l: Peleponnesian earthquake, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The earthquake at Sparta overturned houses, brought down walls, killed more than twenty thousand people, and swallowed household goods and riches.

l: Helots, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Helots joined the Messenians in a league against Sparta after the earthquake weakened the city. They later made daily incursions into Laconia from a fort in Messenia.

l: Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Messenians joined the Helots in attacking Sparta after the earthquake. They continued the war from a fort in Messenia and later joined the revolt of the Helots against the Lacedaemonians.

l: Archidamus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Archidamus, king of Sparta, preserved many citizens by leading them into the open field during the earthquake. He then organized them for the defense of Sparta and its territory.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Lacedaemonians fought the Helots and Messenians and besieged Ithome with their confederates. They dismissed the Athenian forces because they suspected that Athens favored the Messenians.

l: Ithome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Ithome was besieged by the Lacedaemonians and their confederates during the war with the Helots and Messenians. The conflict continued for ten years without deciding the controversy.

l: war of the Helots and Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Helots and Messenians attacked Sparta after the earthquake and later operated from a fort in Messenia. The Lacedaemonians besieged Ithome, but after ten years the war remained undecided.

l: Argives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Argives attacked Mycenae with a large army after the Spartans became unable to assist it. They conquered the city, enslaved its citizens, dedicated a tenth of the spoil to the god, and destroyed Mycenae.

l: Mycenaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Mycenaeans refused to submit to Argive government and supported the Lacedaemonians at Thermopylae. After defending their city for a time, famine forced them to surrender to the Argives.

l: Mycenae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Mycenae was an independent city that claimed ancient renown and disputed religious privileges with Argos. It was besieged, conquered, and razed to the ground by the Argives.

l: destruction of Mycenae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The destruction of Mycenae followed a siege by the Argives. Its citizens were taken captive, its wealth was partly dedicated to the god, and the city was left waste and forsaken.

l: Hiero, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Hiero, king of Syracuse, advised the sons of Anaxilaus to take control from their tutor Micythus. He died at Catana after reigning eleven years and left the kingdom to his brother Thrasybulus.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Syracuse revolted against Thrasybulus because of his cruelty, killings, banishments, and confiscations. After his defeat, the city restored democracy and lived in peace and prosperity for three hundred years until the reign of Dionysius.

l: Micythus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Micythus gave a full and honest account of his administration to the sons of Anaxilaus. Although they asked him to resume governing, he refused, left Rhegium, and settled at Tegea in Arcadia.

l: Gelon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Gelon was remembered as a brave and disciplined ruler who defeated the Carthaginians and governed the Sicilians with moderation and kindness. His reputation restrained revolts during the harsher rule of his brother Hiero.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Thrasybulus succeeded Hiero but ruled with cruelty, ordering killings, false accusations, banishments, and confiscations. A general revolt forced him to surrender the kingdom and depart into exile at Locri.

l: the revolt of the Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: The Syracusans revolted against Thrasybulus and requested aid from Gela, Agrigentum, Selinus, Himera, and other Sicilian cities. With their allies, they defeated him by sea and land and forced him to leave Syracuse.

l: tyranny of Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Thrasybulus's tyranny was marked by cruelty, unlawful killings, banishments, confiscations, and dependence on a standing army and mercenaries. His abuses provoked the people of Syracuse to take up arms against him.

l: democracy of Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: After Thrasybulus departed, the Syracusans removed garrisons from the cities and restored democracy. Syracuse then enjoyed peace and prosperity for three hundred years until the reign of Dionysius.

l: Artabanus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Artabanus, captain of Xerxes' guard, conspired with Mithridates to murder Xerxes and seize the kingdom. He manipulated Artaxerxes into killing Darius, then tried to kill Artaxerxes himself, but Artaxerxes killed him.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Darius, the eldest son of Xerxes, was murdered by Artaxerxes after Artabanus falsely claimed that Darius had killed their father.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Artaxerxes was persuaded by Artabanus to kill his brother Darius and take the Persian throne. When Artabanus later attacked him, Artaxerxes defended himself, killed Artabanus, and became king of Persia.

l: murder of Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIII.
s: Xerxes was murdered in his bedchamber at night by Artabanus with the assistance of Mithridates. Artabanus then attempted to use the murder to place Artaxerxes on the throne.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The unit describes Athenian wars against Aegina, Corinth, Epidaurus, and other opponents, along with the growth of Athenian imperial domination and resistance among its confederates. It recounts the Egyptian revolt from Persia, Athenian aid to Egypt, the Persian expedition, the siege of the White Wall, and the eventual withdrawal of the Athenians from Egypt. It also details civil conflict and political restoration in Sicily, including the struggles at Syracuse, Catana, and other cities. Finally, it covers wars involving Corinth, Megara, the Phocians, the Dorians, and the Lacedaemonians, culminating in the Battle of Tanagra.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Thracians revolted from the Athenians over disputes concerning the mines but were subdued by force. An Athenian colony sent to Amphipolis later suffered defeat when its forces advanced into Thrace and were cut off by the Edones.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenians subdued the Thracians, besieged Aegina, and increasingly ruled their confederates with an imperious authority. They sent aid to the Egyptians, besieged the Persians at the White Wall, and later fought the Corinthians, Epidaurians, Aeginetans, and Lacedaemonians.

l: Aeginetans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Aeginetans rebelled against the Athenians and were besieged after the Athenians invaded their island. They later fought the Athenians at sea but were defeated and forced to submit.

l: Aegina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Aegina was invaded by an Athenian army, which laid waste its countryside and resolved to raze its city. Its defenders later lost a naval battle and submitted to Athens.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Athens expanded its power at sea and exercised increasingly domineering authority over its confederates. It sent fleets to Egypt, besieged the White Wall, and engaged in wars against Aegina, Corinth, Megara, and Sparta.

l: Athenian imperial domination, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: As the Athenians grew powerful, they abandoned their former humanity and courtesy toward their confederates and dominated them with a proud and high hand. This conduct encouraged plans for a general defection.
