l: Athenian confederates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Many of the Athenian confederates began consulting about general defection, while some places decided independently to revolt without waiting for a general assembly.

l: Amphipolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Amphipolis received a colony of ten thousand men sent by the Athenians, drawn partly from citizens and partly from confederates. The colonists divided the surrounding country by lot.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Artaxerxes became king of Persia after the death of Xerxes, punished those involved in his father's murder, reorganized the government, stored provisions, and prepared his forces. He sent armies under Archemenes and later under Artabazus and Megabyzus against Egypt.

l: Xerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Egyptians revolted after hearing of the death of Xerxes and the troubles that followed in Persia.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Persians fought to recover Egypt after the revolt. Their forces were initially defeated by the Egyptians and Athenians, but a later Persian army raised the siege of the White Wall and compelled the Egyptians to submit.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Persia experienced succession troubles after the death of Xerxes, but Artaxerxes restored order and prepared a large military response to the Egyptian revolt.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Egyptians drove Persian treasurers out of Egypt and made Inarus their king. They joined the Athenians against Persia but later submitted when the Persian army reached the White Wall and trapped the Athenian fleet.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Egypt revolted from Persian rule and appealed to Athens for assistance. The country was later invaded by a large Persian army, and the revolt was suppressed after the Egyptians abandoned the Athenians.

l: Inarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Inarus was chosen king by the Egyptians during their revolt from Persia. He raised native and mercenary forces and sent ambassadors to Athens requesting aid.

l: Egyptian revolt from Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Egyptian revolt began after the death of Xerxes and the resulting troubles in Persia. The Egyptians expelled Persian treasurers, established Inarus as king, and sought Athenian military support.

l: Athenian aid to Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenians agreed to aid the Egyptian revolt because they hoped to weaken Persia financially and gain Egypt as an ally. They sent a large fleet, eventually joining the Egyptians in battle.

l: Athenian navy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenians prepared a fleet of three hundred ships for Egypt, though two hundred ships are stated to have arrived there. The fleet was later trapped on Prosopitis after the Persians diverted the river and was burned by the Athenians.

l: Persian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Persian commanders gathered a fleet of three hundred ships in Cilicia and Phoenicia. It sailed along the coast beside the Persian land army to Egypt.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: After the overthrow of royal government, Sicily initially prospered in freedom, peace, and wealth. It later suffered civil wars and seditions before most cities restored their old commonwealths and divided public lands among citizens.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Syracusans fought the mercenaries who had seized parts of Syracuse and eventually defeated them in battle. They also joined Deucetius against Catana and helped restore displaced populations in Sicily.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Syracuse was divided during a conflict between its citizens and foreign mercenaries occupying Acradina and the adjoining island. The Syracusans held another part of the city and eventually defeated the revolters.

l: Sicilian mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The mercenaries enfranchised by Gelon were excluded from magistracies after the restoration of popular government. They seized Acradina and the adjoining island, defended themselves effectively, and were eventually overcome.

l: Gelon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Gelon had enfranchised more than ten thousand mercenaries, over seven thousand of whom remained when the new government excluded them from political honors.

l: Acradina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Acradina was seized and fortified by the revolting mercenaries in Syracuse. The Syracusans repeatedly attacked it but could not immediately drive the revolters out.

l: Syracusan civil war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Syracusan civil war began when mercenaries excluded from office seized Acradina and the adjoining island. The revolters achieved success in skirmishes but were eventually weakened by a lack of provisions.

l: Persian expedition into Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Persian expedition into Egypt was first led by Archemenes and later by Artabazus and Megabyzus. The later army marched through Syria and Phoenicia, raised the siege of the White Wall, and defeated the Egyptian-Athenian resistance through strategy.

l: White Wall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The White Wall sheltered the surviving Persian forces after their defeat by the Egyptians and Athenians. It endured a year-long Athenian siege before the arrival of the new Persian army.

l: Athenians' siege of the White Wall, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Athenians besieged the Persians at the White Wall for about a year. The siege was lifted when Artabazus and Megabyzus arrived with a large army.

l: Artabazus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Artabazus was appointed by Artaxerxes to command the renewed Persian expedition against Egypt with Megabyzus. He helped raise the siege of the White Wall and negotiated the safe withdrawal of the Athenians.

l: Megabyzus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: Megabyzus commanded the renewed Persian expedition against Egypt alongside Artabazus. He participated in the strategy that trapped the Athenian fleet and agreed to let the Athenians leave Egypt without harm.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. XIX.
s: The Lacedaemonians refused Persian money and proposals to attack Athens during the Egyptian revolt. They later sent forces under Nicomedes to aid the Dorians against the Phocians and fought the Athenians at Tanagra.
